title: Dispersion and Colour
kicker: Cambridge Lower Secondary · Science 0893 · Stage 8 · Physics
summary: How a prism shows that white light is a mixture of colours, and how colours of light are added, subtracted by filters, absorbed and reflected to give objects their colour.

blocks.title: In the curriculum
items: Know that **white light is a mixture of many colours**, and that this can be shown by passing white light through a **prism** (dispersion). (8Ps.03)
Describe how colours of light can be **added** (mixed), **subtracted** (by filters), **absorbed** and **reflected** — and use this to explain the colours of objects and filters. (8Ps.04)
Thinking and Working Scientifically used on this page: making predictions from scientific knowledge (8TWSp.03) and presenting observations in tables (8TWSa.05).

blocks.text: 2. White light is a mixture of colours

Light from the Sun or a bright lamp looks white, but it is really a **mixture of many colours**. You can show this with a glass **prism**: shine a narrow beam of white light into one side and a band of colours comes out of the other side. This splitting of white light into colours is called **dispersion**, and the band of colours is called a **spectrum**.

blocks.alt: A glass prism splitting a beam of white light into a band of colours
blocks.caption: A glass prism disperses white light into a spectrum, from red (bent least) to violet (bent most).

blocks.text: The colours always appear in the same order: **red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet**. A memory sentence: **R**ichard **O**f **Y**ork **G**ave **B**attle **I**n **V**ain (ROYGBIV). The colours blend smoothly into one another — the spectrum is continuous, and the seven names are just the main colours we name.
3. Why does a prism split white light?

You learned in the reflection and refraction lesson that light **slows down** when it enters glass, and bends towards the normal. The key extra fact is that **each colour slows down by a different amount** in glass:

items: **Violet** light slows down the **most**, so it is refracted (bent) the **most**.
**Red** light slows down the **least**, so it is refracted the **least**.

All the other colours are in between, so they spread out in order. The light is refracted at both faces of the prism, and because the faces are not parallel the colours spread out even more as they leave.

blocks.text: In a rectangular glass block the two faces are parallel, so the colours bend back the way they came and come out almost on top of each other — that is why you do not usually see a spectrum from a window.
4. Evidence: the colours come from the white light, not the prism
Someone might suggest that the prism **adds** colour to the light, like a coloured filter. Isaac Newton tested this idea with **two prisms**:

items: A first prism splits white light into a spectrum.

Newton let only one colour (for example red) pass through a slit into a second prism. The red light was bent again but stayed **red** — the prism did not change its colour, so the prism does not make colours.
Then he placed a second prism **upside down** in the path of the whole spectrum. The colours were bent back together and **white light** came out.
Conclusion: the colours were in the white light all along. The prism only **separates** them (and a second prism can **recombine** them).

blocks.text: This is a good example of how evidence can support one idea (white light is a mixture) and contradict another (the prism adds colour).

blocks.title: Rainbows
blocks.text: A rainbow is dispersion in nature. Sunlight enters raindrops, is refracted, reflects off the back of the drop and is refracted again as it leaves. Each colour is bent by a different amount, so you see a spectrum. You can only see a rainbow when the Sun is **behind** you and the rain is in front of you.

blocks.alt: A rainbow arching over green fields under a cloudy sky
blocks.caption: A rainbow: sunlight is dispersed by raindrops, so red is on the outside of the arc and violet on the inside.

blocks.text: 5. Adding colours of light

The **primary colours of light** are **red, green and blue**. By mixing (adding) these three in different amounts, you can make light of any colour. Screens on phones, laptops and TVs work this way: every pixel is made of tiny red, green and blue parts.

blocks.text: Yellow, magenta and cyan are the **secondary colours of light**. Notice that adding a secondary colour to the primary colour it is missing also gives white: yellow + blue = white, cyan + red = white, magenta + green = white.

blocks.title: Light is not paint
blocks.text: Mixing **paints** is different from mixing **lights**. Red paint and green paint mixed give a muddy brown, not yellow, because paints **absorb** colours (each paint takes away some colours, so the mixture reflects less light). With lights, colours are **added**, so the mixture gets brighter. In Checkpoint questions about light, never use paint rules.
6. Subtracting colours: filters

A coloured **filter** is a transparent sheet that **transmits** (lets through) only its own colour and **absorbs** all the other colours. It **subtracts** colours from white light — it cannot add any colour that was not already there.

blocks.text: **Two filters:** work step by step. The first filter decides what reaches the second filter. The second filter can only let through colours that are **in that light and** that it transmits. For example: white light → yellow filter → red and green come out → green filter → only **green** comes out.
7. Why objects have colour: reflecting and absorbing
Most objects do not make their own light. We see them because they **reflect** light into our eyes. The colour of an opaque object depends on which colours it reflects and which colours it absorbs:

items: A **red** object reflects red light and absorbs the other colours.
A **white** object reflects **all** colours.
A **black** object absorbs **all** colours and reflects none (that is why black things get hot in sunlight).
A **yellow** object reflects red and green (and yellow) and absorbs blue; a **cyan** object reflects green and blue; a **magenta** object reflects red and blue.

blocks.text: **Coloured light on coloured objects.** An object can only reflect colours that are **in the light shining on it**. Use this method:

items: Write down which colours are in the light (white = red + green + blue).
Write down which colours the object can reflect.
The object looks the colour of what is in **both** lists. If nothing is in both, it looks **black**.

blocks.title: القاعدة اللي لازم تحفظها
items: الضوء الأبيض = خليط من كل الألوان. المنشور بيفصلها (تشتت) وهو مش بيضيف ألوان.
البنفسجي بينكسر أكتر حاجة، والأحمر أقل حاجة.
جمع ضوء: أحمر + أخضر = أصفر، أحمر + أزرق = أرجواني (magenta)، أخضر + أزرق = سماوي (cyan)، والتلاتة = أبيض.
الفلتر بيعدّي لونه بس ويمتص الباقي.
الجسم بيعكس لونه ويمتص الباقي — ولو اللون ده مش موجود في الضوء اللي نازل عليه يبان أسود.

blocks.text: 8. Worked examples
**Worked example 1** — Describe how you could show that white light is made of different colours. [2]

items: Shine a narrow beam of white light (from a ray box) into a glass prism (1).
A spectrum of colours (red to violet) appears on a white screen on the other side — the white light has been dispersed into its colours (1).
**Common mistake:** writing only "use a prism". Say what you do **and** what you observe.

blocks.text: **Worked example 2** — In the spectrum from a prism, which colour is refracted most? Explain why. [2]

items: **Violet** (1).
Violet light slows down the most when it enters the glass, so it changes direction the most (1).

blocks.text: **Worked example 3** — A red spotlight and a green spotlight shine on the same part of a white wall. (a) What colour does the wall look where they overlap? [1] (b) A blue spotlight is added to the same place. What colour is it now? [1]

items: (a) red + green = **yellow**.
(b) red + green + blue = **white**.
**Common mistake:** answering "brown" — that is mixing paint, not light.

blocks.text: **Worked example 4** — White light passes through a magenta filter and then through a blue filter. What colour comes out? Explain. [2]

items: The magenta filter transmits **red and blue** and absorbs green (1).
The blue filter transmits blue and absorbs red, so only **blue** light comes out (1).

blocks.text: **Worked example 5** — A footballer's kit has a **yellow** shirt and **blue** shorts. On a dark evening the pitch is lit only by red light. Predict the colour of the shirt and shorts. Explain. [3]

items: Shirt looks **red**: yellow cloth reflects red and green; only red light is present, so it reflects red (1).
Shorts look **black**: blue cloth reflects only blue; there is no blue in red light, so it absorbs all the light (1).
Correct reasoning using reflect / absorb for both (1).

blocks.text: **Worked example 6** — A girl says, "The prism adds the colours to the light, like a filter." Describe an experiment that shows she is wrong. [2]

items: Use a second prism, turned the other way, in the path of the spectrum from the first prism (1).

The colours recombine to make **white** light again, which shows the colours were already in the white light — the prism only separates them (1). (Accept: pass one colour through a second prism — it stays the same colour.)

blocks.title: Common mistakes
items: Saying the prism **makes** or **adds** the colours. It **separates** colours that are already in white light.
Getting the order of the spectrum wrong, or saying red is bent most. **Violet is bent most, red least.**
Using paint rules for light (red + green light is **yellow**, not brown).
Saying a red filter "turns light red". It **absorbs** the other colours and **transmits** red.
Saying a red object "absorbs red". It **reflects** red and **absorbs** the other colours.
Forgetting that an object can only reflect colours that are **in the light shining on it** — otherwise it looks black.
Writing "cyan" or "magenta" as "light blue" or "pink" when the question asks for the name of the colour. Learn the proper names.

blocks.title: How Checkpoint asks this
items: **Label** the colours of the spectrum on a prism diagram, or say which colour is bent most / least.
**Complete** a colour-addition diagram of three overlapping circles of red, green and blue light.
**Predict** what colour comes through one or two filters, or what colour an object looks in coloured light — then **explain** using the words *transmit*, *absorb* and *reflect*.
**Complete a table** of object colours under different coloured lights.
**Describe** an experiment with a prism (what you do, what you see), or evaluate a student's claim using evidence.
Exam technique: in an explanation, say which colours are **absorbed** and which are **reflected/transmitted** — one mark is often for each idea.

blocks.text: Practice

blocks.title: Dispersion and colour — practice
blocks.intro: Answer every part. Type short answers (one colour word) in the box; for longer answers write yours on paper first, then mark it with the mark scheme.

questions.q: A beam of white light shines through a glass prism and a band of colours appears on a screen. What does this show?
c: White light is a mixture of colours.
questions.e: The prism **separates** (disperses) the colours that are already in white light. It does not add colour, and light slows down (not speeds up) in glass.

questions.q: What is the name for the splitting of white light into its colours? [1]
questions.e: Splitting white light into its colours is called **dispersion**. (The band of colours itself is the spectrum.)

questions.q: Which colour of light is refracted **most** by a glass prism?
questions.e: Violet light slows down the most in glass, so it is refracted the most. Red is refracted the least.

questions.q: Which colour comes between **green** and **indigo** in the spectrum? [1]
questions.e: Order: red, orange, yellow, green, **blue**, indigo, violet.

questions.q: (a) What colour of light is seen in region **P**? [1]
questions.e: Region P is where red and green light overlap: red + green = **yellow**.

questions.q: (b) What colour of light is seen in region **R**? [1]
questions.e: Region R is where green and blue overlap: green + blue = **cyan**.
questions.p:
Question 5
Red, green and blue spotlights shine onto a white screen. The circles overlap.

questions.q: (c) What colour of light is seen in region **S**? [1]
questions.e: Region S is where all three primary colours overlap: red + green + blue = **white**.
questions.p:
Question 5
Red, green and blue spotlights shine onto a white screen. The circles overlap.

questions.q: White light shines on a **cyan** filter. Which colours of light pass through it?
questions.e: Cyan = green + blue. A cyan filter **transmits** green and blue and **absorbs** red.

questions.q: White light passes through a **red** filter and then through a **blue** filter. What comes out of the blue filter? [1]
questions.e: The red filter lets through only red. The blue filter absorbs red, so **no light** comes out — it looks black.

questions.q: A green leaf is seen in a room lit only by red light. What colour does it look?
questions.e: A green leaf reflects only green light. Red light contains no green, so the leaf absorbs all the light that hits it and reflects none — it looks **black**.

questions.q: A **white** T-shirt is seen in blue light. What colour does it look? [1]
questions.e: A white object reflects every colour that falls on it. Only blue light falls on it, so it reflects blue and looks **blue**.

questions.q: A **yellow** banana is lit by **green** light. What colour does it look?
questions.e: Yellow objects reflect red and green light (and absorb blue). Only green light falls on the banana, so it reflects green and looks **green**.

questions.q: Explain why a red rose looks red in white light. Use the words **reflects** and **absorbs** in your answer. [2]
questions.ms: 1 mark: the rose (petals) reflects red light (into our eyes). 1 mark: it absorbs all the other colours / green and blue. Do not accept 'it absorbs red'. Do not accept 'it gives out red light'.
questions.e: White light contains all colours. The red petals **reflect** the red light into our eyes (1) and **absorb** all the other colours (1), so only red light reaches us from the rose.

questions.q: A student says: "A prism makes the colours." Describe an experiment with **two** prisms that shows the colours were already in the white light. State what you would observe. [3]
questions.ms: 1 mark: use a first prism to make a spectrum from white light. 1 mark: place a second prism, turned the other way (upside down), in the path of the spectrum. 1 mark: the colours recombine / white light comes out, so the colours were already in the white light. Alternative for marks 2–3: let only one colour through a slit into the second prism (1); it stays the same colour / no new colours appear (1).
questions.e: Use the first prism to disperse white light into a spectrum (1). Put a second, identical prism the opposite way round in the path of the spectrum (1). White light comes out of the second prism — the colours have been recombined, so they were in the white light all along and the prism only separates them (1).

blocks.title: Remember
items: White light is a mixture of colours. A prism **disperses** it into a spectrum: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet.
Each colour slows down by a different amount in glass: **violet is refracted most, red least**.
Primary colours of light: **red, green, blue**. Red + green = yellow, red + blue = magenta, green + blue = cyan, all three = white.
A filter **transmits** its own colour(s) and **absorbs** the rest — it subtracts colours.
An object **reflects** its own colour(s) and **absorbs** the rest. White reflects all; black absorbs all.
An object can only reflect colours that are in the light shining on it; if there are none, it looks **black**.
